 Retired couple's Medicare costs triple after move to a Minnesota county without Medicare Advantage plan options in 2027
 Vawn Himmelsbach Sat, November 21, 2026 at 12:00 PM MST 6 min read Rix Pix Photography/Shutterstock If you're planning to retire in another state, you might be considering factors such as state taxes and homeowners insurance as part of your budget. But Medicare could turn out to be a surprise expense you weren't planning for. 
 That's what one retired couple discovered, after a move from Rochester, New York, to Crow Wing County, Minnesota.

 Steve Myhro, 71, is a retired teacher who moved to Minnesota with his wife Sarah, 68, to be closer to family. But they had no idea their Medicare Advantage costs would jump by as much as $7,000 a year — from $2,900 to more than $9,000. 
 Ironically, they wouldn't have had the same problem in other nearby counties. 
 "I could have built the house five miles away in Cass County and not be experiencing these kinds of increases. To me, that just makes no sense," Steve told MPR News . 
 That's because, starting in 2027, Medicare enrollees in Crow Wing, Wadena and Lake of the Woods will have no Medicare Advantage plan options to choose from, thanks to restructuring by health insurers — often forcing them to purchase much more expensive alternatives. 
 Across the U.S., 187 counties will have no Medicare Advantage options in 2027 — which could be a financial blow to seniors on a fixed budget. 
 Why some retirees will pay more 
 Medicare Advantage is the private plan alternative to Original Medicare. But it's only available at the county level. 
 Insurers who serve the Medicare Advantage market blame rising medical and pharmaceutical costs for their financial losses, which they say is pressuring them to restructure their offerings — especially in rural areas where it's harder to maintain provider networks. 
 In 2027, 193 counties will have no Medicare Advantage prescription drug (MD-PD) plan options available, according to an analysis by KFF . That's a big jump from 2026, when 123 counties had no MA-PDs available. This will impact 1% of all Medicare beneficiaries — or 638,000 Americans. 
 In six of those counties, a Medicare Advantage plan is still available, just without drug coverage. 
 "But in the other 187 counties, no Medicare Advantage plans with or without prescription drug coverage for general enrollment are available," according to KFF. 
 Story Continues Counties are impacted in 16 states, including Minnesota. The others include Alaska, California, Colorado, Idaho, Kansas, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Utah and Vermont, as well as all U.S. territories except Puerto Rico. 
 Alaska stands out, since no MA-PDs are offered in any county in the state. 
 The Myhros originally had coverage through Blue Cross Blue Shield of Minnesota, which cost a combined $2,900 annually. But now it's no longer offered — and there are no other Medicare Advantage plans to choose from. In Crow Wing County, about 1 in 4 residents is 65+ , according to Census data. 
 The Myhros' insurance broker recommended they add a separate drug plan and Medigap to Original Medicare to fill in coverage holes, which will cost the couple more than $9,000 a year. 
 "I really want to know why we as seniors are having to bear so much of the cost of this kind of market restructuring," Steve told MPR News.

 What to do if this happens to you 
 Medicare Advantage plans are dynamic, which means they're updated from year to year. So you can't just 'set it and forget it.' 
 For example, you might discover that your plan's offerings have changed, out-of-pocket maximums have increased or dental and vision benefits have been reduced. Even the provider network — the doctors and hospitals you have access to — can change. 
 Or your plan might no longer be available. 
 This year, Medicare's annual enrollment period ends on Dec. 7. During this period, you can enroll in Medicare or modify your existing coverage for 2027. Changes go into effect on Jan. 1. 
 However, if your Medicare Advantage plan has been discontinued, you likely qualify for the Special Enrollment Period (SEP), which gives you some extra time to select an option for next year. That runs from Dec. 8 through the end of February. But keep in mind that could leave you with gaps in coverage at the start of the new year. 
 If your Medicare Advantage plan has been discontinued, check if other plans are available in your county. If there are no longer any plan options, you can return to Original Medicare (Parts A and B), adding a Part D drug plan and applying for a Medigap supplement. 
 If you do nothing, your Medicare Advantage coverage will default to Original Medicare (Parts A and B), but you'll have to enroll in Part D so you don't lose your prescription drug coverage in 2027. 
 You might also want to consider Medigap (Medicare Supplement Insurance), which helps with out-of-pocket costs like coinsurance and deductibles. If your MA-PD is no longer offered in 2027, look for a Medigap policy with guaranteed issue rights, which means you can't be denied coverage or charged more based on your health conditions. 
 If you need help navigating your options, your local State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) provides one-on-one insurance counseling and assistance with Medicare. You can also contact an independent Medicare agent in your area, who represents multiple carriers. 
 And, if you're planning to move, check the Medicare Advantage options available in your retirement destination. If the options are already limited, you'll have less recourse if plans change or are discontinued. Maybe moving just five miles away to another county could save you a lot of headaches down the road.
